name: Carlos Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you start by telling me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work a stamping press at a factory that makes metal panels for washing machines. A big sheet of steel goes in, the press comes down with about four hundred tonnes, and out comes a side panel with all the holes punched. I load blanks, check the first-off panel against the gauge, and stack the good ones in stillages, which are big metal cages. Seven months in, and I'm still the slowest on the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple. You do it right, the panel's right, you go home. What wears me out is the ear defenders all day and the supervisor shouting numbers at us after every break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is not much. Maybe I'd tell the lads it was like those 3D televisions everyone was meant to buy. I don't post online, I don't really do any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing. My press doesn't care about chatbots. I own my flat outright, because my aunt left it to me, so I've got no rent, and I've got a fair bit saved on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up, keep my head down, try to get my speed up so the supervisor stops picking on me. Maybe put a bit more aside each month. I wouldn't change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how I like things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the slowest on the line. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. There's a review at the one-year mark, and they could let me go if I'm still slow. But there are three other press shops on the industrial estate, so I'd just walk across the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your extra savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing clever. They sit in the bank. My brother keeps telling me to buy shares, but I don't trust anything I can't see.

say: I'd compare AI to **3D televisions**, another thing everyone was meant to buy.
I wouldn't **post online**, because I don't really do any of that.
think: Privately, my **press** doesn't care about chatbots, so nothing changes.
I own my flat **outright** from my aunt and have savings on top.
do: Keep his head down and raise his **press speed** before the one-year review.
Put a little more into the **bank** each month.
feel: He feels **calm**, which is how he likes things.
S0.quote: My press doesn't care about chatbots.
fieldNote: An inherited flat with **no rent** makes him unusually secure for a junior worker.
His only worry is the **one-year review**, and other press shops are across the road.
He distrusts **shares** and anything he can't see.

steps.text: Get faster on the panel press before the one-year review
Add a little more to the bank account each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who need to worry, not us. I'd probably say it at break and leave it there. I'm not one for arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine for a good while. Robots spreading slowly means maybe one new robot cell every couple of years, and they'll put it on the newer presses first. The people buying the steel and planning the shifts are the ones whose desks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, keep going. If they brought in a robot to stack the panels, I'd ask to stay on the old press. I wouldn't go on any course unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe I'd notice it a bit more, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask to stay on the old press. What if the old press goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd move to another factory that still has old presses. There's always a smaller shop that can't afford the fancy kit, and I'd rather do that than learn to babysit a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the lady in the planning office, Sandra, who does the shift rotas. Everything she does is on a computer, so a program could do it. I'd feel bad for her, she always brings cake on Fridays.

say: I'd say it's the **office lot** who need to worry, not press workers.
I'd mention it at **break** and leave it there, without arguing.
think: Robots spreading slowly means maybe one **robot cell** every couple of years, newer presses first.
The people **buying steel** and planning shifts are the ones whose desks change.
do: Ask to stay on the **old press** if a stacking robot comes in.
Avoid **courses** unless the firm makes them compulsory.
feel: He feels **calm**, noticing it more but not losing **sleep**.
S1.quote: There's always a smaller shop that can't afford the fancy kit, and I'd rather do that than learn to babysit a robot.
fieldNote: He correctly sees **desk work** shifting first and slow robots giving him time.
His fallback is to move to **smaller shops** with older kit, not to learn.
He shows warmth for an office colleague whose **rota work** is exposed.

steps.text: Ask to stay on the old panel press if robots arrive
Move to a smaller press shop with older kit if needed
Skip any course unless the firm makes it compulsory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and nobody voted for it. At work I'd say they'll still need someone to clean up after the robots. I'd probably not say much else, because I don't know enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2031 I think my job's done. The AI in 2028 won't bother me, but a robot that loads a press and checks a panel is easy, and they'd have those in three years. The smaller shops would get them too once they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd talk to my brother. He runs a small roofing business, and robots on roofs feel a long way off. I'd keep the press job until 2030 for the money, then move to roofing with him. I'd stop spending on anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be okay for money, with the flat, but I'd hate starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd avoid any course. Is roofing a kind of starting over too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, yeah. But it's my brother, and he'd show me himself. Learning off family is different from some trainer with slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much to cut, honestly. I'd stop the football season ticket and not replace my van. With no rent, I could live on half my pay for a long time.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and nobody voted for it.
At work I'd say they'll still need someone to **clean up** after the robots.
think: The **2028 AI** won't bother me, but loading-and-checking robots are easy by **2031**.
Even the **smaller shops** would get robots once they're cheap.
do: Keep the press job until **2030** for the money.
Move into his brother's **roofing business**, learning from him directly.
Drop the **season ticket** and don't replace his van.
feel: He feels **anxious**, safe for money with the flat but hating **starting over**.
S2.quote: Learning off family is different from some trainer with slides.
fieldNote: He resists **formal courses** but would learn a new trade from his brother.
He spots that robots arriving three years later still **reach** his loading-and-checking job.
No rent means he could live on **half his pay**, which steadies him.

steps.text: Join his brother's roofing business around 2030
Learn roofing from his brother rather than a formal course
Give up the football season ticket and keep the old van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really. I'd say firms will do what firms do, and the government will be late as usual. I'm not angry at anyone, it's just how things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years means I'd probably drift. I'd stay on the press until 2033 because it pays well, and only move when I see the robot in the building. That's probably a mistake, but that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the press job and keep saving. Start helping my brother on roofs on Saturdays, so I'm not starting from zero. Not do anything with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a slower kind. Like I know there's a bill coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Saturdays on the roofs. When would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the summer before the robots show up, so 2033. My brother would say start now, and he'd be right. I'd still wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you're not angry at anyone. Really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little at the bosses who'll get rich off it. But I'd buy the cheap robot too if I owned the factory, so you can't blame people for doing sums.

say: I'd say **firms** will do what firms do and the government will be **late**.
I'm not **angry** at anyone; it's just how things go.
think: With five years, I'd probably **drift** and stay on the press until 2033.
I'd only move when I see the **robot** in the building, which is probably a mistake.
do: Keep the press job and keep **saving** until around 2033.
Help his brother on **roofs on Saturdays** from about 2033.
feel: He feels a slow **anxiety**, like a **bill** that's coming.
S3.quote: I'd buy the cheap robot too if I owned the factory, so you can't blame people for doing sums.
fieldNote: His **centre** view shows: he blames nobody much, even the bosses.
He predicts his own **delay** and admits it's probably a mistake.
His safety net is **family**, not training schemes.

steps.text: Stay on the panel press until about 2033
Keep saving while the press pay is good
Work Saturdays on his brother's roofing jobs from 2033

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots could happen. I'd probably not say much at all, if I'm honest. People talk too much about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels far off. By 2039 I'd be 40 and could have done ten years of roofing by then if I wanted. Or the robots might be late, like trains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep pressing panels for a few years, then probably go over to roofing with my brother around 2032. Keep the savings in the bank. Maybe get the flat redone while I'm still on good money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. It's far enough away that I don't think about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots might be late. What if they're early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to my brother sooner. That's the nice thing about having family with a business. I'm lucky, a lot of the lads don't have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the lads would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones with kids and rent. I've got no kids and no rent, so I can sit tight, and the lads with both can't.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and lots could happen.
I'd probably say very little, because people **talk too much** about the future.
think: By **2039** I could have done years of roofing with my brother.
The robots might even be **late**, like trains.
do: Keep pressing panels until about **2032**, then join his brother's roofing firm.
Get the **flat redone** while still on good money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years isn't long to learn roofing properly, and my brother can't take on everyone. What would help is decent notice from the firm, a year at least, so I can plan the switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the sound of a good panel dropping out of the press. Nobody gets a buzz out of a robot doing it for them.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the sound of a good panel dropping out of the press.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** stamping press operator making washing machine panels, seven months in.
He owns his **flat outright** from his aunt and keeps savings in the bank.
He avoids new technology and **courses**, and blames nobody much for change.
His **brother's roofing** business is his plan B as AGI and robots get closer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **three years** is too short to learn roofing properly.
whatWouldHelp: At least a **year's notice** from the firm so he can plan the switch.
